records.quote: I am almost a whole day old, now.  I arrived yesterday.
records.paraphrase: The narrator describes having just come into existence a day ago.

records.quote: I have experimented and experimented until now I know it never does run uphill, except in the dark.  I know it does in the dark, because the pool never goes dry
records.paraphrase: The narrator's mistaken reasoning about water running uphill contrasts with reader knowledge.

records.quote: It gave me a thrill, for it was the first time I had ever heard speech, except my own.
records.paraphrase: The narrator is thrilled to hear another being speak for the first time.

records.quote: It has no hips; it tapers like a carrot; when it stands, it spreads itself apart like a derrick; so I think it is a reptile, though it may be architecture.
records.paraphrase: The narrator's naive classification of a man as possibly a reptile contrasts with the reader's knowledge.

records.quote: I was curious to know what the pink dust was.  Suddenly the name of it occurred to me, though I had never heard of it before.  It was FIRE!
records.paraphrase: The narrator identifies and names the newly produced substance as fire.

records.quote: I followed the other Experiment around, yesterday afternoon, at a distance, to see what it might be for, if I could.
records.paraphrase: The narrator observes another creature to determine its purpose.

records.quote: When I look back, the Garden is a dream to me.  It was beautiful, surpassingly beautiful, enchantingly beautiful; and now it is lost, and I shall not see it any more.
records.paraphrase: The narrator describes the loss of the Garden after the Fall.

records.quote: I have seen some of the best ones melt and run down the sky. Since one can melt, they can all melt
records.paraphrase: The narrator's belief that stars melt contrasts with the reader's understanding of stars.

records.quote: I had created something that didn't exist before; I had added a new thing to the world's uncountable properties
records.paraphrase: The narrator recognizes she has introduced fire, a new thing, into the world.

records.quote: It is best to prove things by actual experiment; then you KNOW; whereas if you depend on guessing and supposing and conjecturing, you never get educated.
records.paraphrase: The narrator articulates a method of proving things by experiment rather than conjecture.

records.quote: In the rush of finishing up yesterday, the mountains were left in a ragged condition, and some of the plains were so cluttered with rubbish and remnants that the aspects were quite distressing.
records.paraphrase: The narrator describes a newly created world still being finished and tidied.

records.quote: When they first showed, last night, I tried to knock some down with a pole, but it didn't reach, which astonished me; then I tried clods till I was all tired out, but I never got one.
records.paraphrase: The narrator attempts to reach the stars physically and learns they are unreachable.

records.quote: FEAR.  And it is horrible!--I wish I had never discovered it; it gives me dark moments, it spoils my happiness, it makes me shiver and tremble and shudder.
records.paraphrase: The narrator describes discovering and being distressed by the new emotion of fear.

records.quote: For I feel like an experiment, I feel exactly like an experiment; it would be impossible for a person to feel more like an experiment than I do, and so I am coming to feel convinced that that is what I AM--an experiment; just an experiment, and nothing more.
records.paraphrase: The narrator reflects on her own nature and concludes she is an experiment.

records.quote: I laid a dry stick on the ground and tried to bore a hole in it with another one, in order to carry out a scheme that I had
records.paraphrase: The narrator experiments by boring a hole to produce an effect.

records.quote: When the mighty brontosaurus came striding into camp, she regarded it as an acquisition, I considered it a calamity
records.paraphrase: A brontosaurus appears in the story's world, placing it in a prehistoric or mythical setting.

records.quote: The moon got loose last night, and slid down and fell out of the scheme--a very great loss
records.paraphrase: The moon is described as coming loose and falling out of its place in the sky.

records.quote: I learned a lesson; also I made an axiom, all out of my own head--my very first one; THE SCRATCHED EXPERIMENT SHUNS THE THORN.
records.paraphrase: The narrator forms a generalized rule from her experience with thorns.

records.quote: By experiment I know that wood swims, and dry leaves, and feathers, and plenty of other things; therefore by all that cumulative evidence you know that a rock will swim
records.paraphrase: The narrator reasons by cumulative evidence from experiments, drawing a faulty conclusion.

criteria.rationale: Natural phenomena (fire, stars, distances, buoyancy) are named and reasoned about, but the treatment is naive and satirical rather than a material scientific representation; the narrator's conclusions (stars melting, rocks swimming, water running uphill) are deliberately wrong, so the scientific content is more comedic device than genuine science.

The discovery/naming of fire is a natural process and personal wonder, not an engineered device, technique, or invention that materially shapes the setting, problem, or outcome. No technology or invention drives the story.

The story is set in a mythic/remote past: the freshly created world of Eden with a brontosaurus roaming the camp, placing the narrative in a prehistoric/primordial setting rather than the ordinary present.

The premise of a newly created being discovering the world yields consequences (the creation of fire as a new thing, the loss of the Garden after the Fall), but these are more mythic/narrative developments than systematic extrapolation from an identifiable premise.

Eve repeatedly and explicitly champions proof by experiment over conjecture, forms axioms, tests hypotheses (water uphill, buoyancy, distances), and revises understanding through observation; the scientific method is a central, sustained motif of her diary.
The setting is a terrestrial Garden of Eden. Stars and moon are observed from Earth but there is no other planet, dimension, nonordinary cosmic environment, or visitor from such a place.

The Fall and expulsion from Eden is a large-scale, world-altering loss remembered by the narrator, and Eve fears the stars will all melt away; these carry a catastrophic register but are mythic/cosmic-comic rather than a concretely realized disaster central to the plot's action.

candidates.description: The story is set in a freshly created, still-being-finished world (Eden/Garden) in which cosmological and natural features are literal artifacts of a recent act of creation: mountains left ragged, plains cluttered, the moon coming loose and falling out of the sky, and stars that can be reached at the rim of the circle. This totalizing 'newly-minted cosmos' frames the narrator's entire existence and epistemology.

novelty.rationale: The world is presented as a recently constructed artifact, materially different from the empirical norm: mountains are 'left in a ragged condition' after a rush of finishing, and the moon literally 'got loose' and 'fell out of the scheme.' This is a totalizing difference altering the story universe's cosmology.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The created-world premise draws on a religious/mythic creation frame (the Garden, the Fall) rather than an immanent nonsupernatural account. The 'scheme,' the makers who return the moon, and the Giver point to a supernatural rather than systematic imaginary-science logic, leaving cognitive validation uncertain.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The freshly-created world governs the whole narrative: the diary form, the naming of creatures, the naive cosmology, and ultimately the loss of the Garden after the Fall all flow from this premise.

estrangement.rationale: The narrator's literal beliefs (moon falling out, stars melting, water running uphill in the dark) contrast sharply with reader knowledge of empirical physics, producing estrangement through a defamiliarized cosmos.

candidates.description: The narrator is a being who came into existence 'a day ago' and constructs knowledge of the entire world from scratch through observation, experiment, naming, and axiom-formation. She invents empirical method (proving by experiment), names all creatures instantly, and identifies fire as a wholly new thing she has created.

novelty.rationale: A one-day-old adult consciousness building all knowledge from zero, naming every creature as 'the first,' and literally 'adding a new thing to the world' (fire) departs totally from the empirical norm of gradual human development.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The narrator develops a coherent, systematic (if error-prone) empirical methodology: forming axioms, insisting on demonstration, and reasoning from cumulative evidence. This is an immanent, nonsupernatural cognitive process even where conclusions are faulty.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The entire text is the first-person record of this newborn cognizing narrator; her process of discovery, naming, and experiment structures every episode and constitutes the narrative's overriding logic.

estrangement.rationale: The reader recognizes fire, men, stars, and hydrology that the newborn narrator misidentifies (a man as a reptile, stars that melt, water running uphill in the dark), estranging familiar things through the eyes of a first cognizer.

candidates.description: The narrator accidentally produces fire by boring a stick, recognizes it as a wholly new thing, and reflects that she has 'added a new thing to the world's uncountable properties.'

novelty.rationale: Fire is presented as literally the first fire, smoke, and flames ever to exist in the world, a new property added to the universe.

cognitive_validation.rationale: Fire arises through an immanent, nonsupernatural mechanical process (boring a dry stick), a coherent causal account.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: Fire is a single memorable episode and a device revealing character contrast; it does not determine the overriding narrative logic, which is driven by the narrator's cognition and the relationship with Adam. It is incidental relative to the whole diary.

estrangement.rationale: The reader knows fire as commonplace, but the narrator's wonder at its first-ever appearance and her discovery of fear through it defamiliarizes it.
